name: Shag

card.summary: The shag is a layered, feathered, choppy haircut that adds movement and volume and softens the face outline.

quick.overview:
The shag is a layered haircut that is feathered at the top and sides, full around the crown and thinned into fringes at the edges. It is generally credited to New York hairstylist Paul McGregor, who reportedly gave it to Jane Fonda around 1969.

The style gained fame after the 1971 film Klute and became a popular unisex look in the early 1970s. It has returned repeatedly since, including the wolf cut, a shorter-fronted variant popular in the 2020s.
quick.how: A stylist cuts layers of varied length through the hair, with feathered ends and often a fringe. It is worn tousled and textured. Variants such as the wolf cut are shorter at the front with bangs.
quick.risks: There are no health risks specific to the cut. Results depend on hair type and density, and layered cuts grow out unevenly.

lead: The shag is a layered haircut in which the layers are feathered at the top and sides, giving fullness around the crown and thin, fringe-like ends at the edges.[1] People choose it to add volume, movement and texture to their hair and to frame the face with soft, choppy edges rather than a single blunt line. It is a unisex style and is usually worn tousled rather than sleek.[1]

The cut is usually credited to New York hairstylist Paul McGregor, who reportedly gave it to Jane Fonda around 1969 and first called it the Funky; the word shag was already in print as a hairstyle name by 1956.[1] It became widely known after Fonda wore it in the 1971 film Klute, was taken up by musicians through the early 1970s, and has returned in several later waves, most recently in the early 2020s alongside the wolf cut, a shorter-fronted, mullet-like variant.[1][2]

Because the style is defined by how the hair is cut rather than by any product or procedure, its effect on appearance is immediate and visible at the salon. Layered cuts in general are described as creating the look of both length and volume, with shorter top layers adding lift and longer lengths underneath preserving length.[4] No published studies have examined the shag as a haircut.

chain: Stylist cuts feathered layers and a fringe
Hair gains lift, volume and texture at the crown and sides
Face outline looks softer and more framed
angle.text: The layered cut reshapes the volume and outline of the hair, framing the face with feathered fringes. The change is visible as soon as the cut is finished and then grows out gradually.

infobox: Wolf cut; related to The Rachel[1][3]

paras: A shag is built from layers of different lengths cut through the hair. The layers are feathered at the top and sides, which makes the hair look full around the crown, and they taper into thin, fringe-like ends around the edges.[1] The result is a deliberately uneven, tousled outline, as opposed to a one-length cut.

Layering in general changes how hair sits. A description of layered haircuts says shorter top layers blend into the longer layers beneath them, so the cut can read as both long and voluminous, and that the layers can be distinct or softly blended.[4] The same description lists two common cutting approaches: a sliding cut that suits medium wavy hair and blended elevation, which it says works best on straight or slightly wavy hair rather than wavy or curly hair.[4]

The wolf cut is the best-known modern variant. It is shorter at the front, resembles a mullet and often includes bangs.[1] The mullet itself is described as short at the front, top and sides and long at the back, and its article notes that mullets of the early 1970s, worn by figures such as David Bowie and Paul McCartney, were close to the shag that David Cassidy and Rod Stewart popularised.[2]

The Rachel, the layered style Jennifer Aniston wore on Friends, is often described as a blend of a shag and a bob. It has voluminous, feathered, choppy layers that frame the face and flick outward, usually ends just above the collarbone and includes a side-parted fringe.[3]

Paul McGregor is usually credited with creating the cut, which he reportedly gave to Jane Fonda around 1969 under the name the Funky.[1] The word shag was nevertheless already in print for a hairstyle by 1956, so the name predates his version.[1]

The cut became famous after Fonda wore it in the 1971 film Klute.[1] During the early 1970s it was worn by Joan Jett, David Bowie, Mick Jagger, Rod Stewart, David Cassidy, Stevie Nicks and Florence Henderson, which tied it closely to rock and film culture.[1]

Chris McMillan created The Rachel, which Aniston first wore in the first season of Friends, with her debut of the look in an episode aired in April 1995.[3] It became a global trend and was described in one trade publication as the most requested haircut of the decade; a 2004 poll named it the most influential haircut of all time.[3] Meg Ryan wore a shag in the early 2000s.[1]

The shag returned to popularity in the early 2020s, and fashion press in 2021 covered the wolf cut as a summer take on it.[1] The wolf cut has been associated with Billie Eilish, Camila Cabello and Miley Cyrus.[1] Mullet-style cuts were also described as having a wider revival from 2020, with i-D calling 2020 the year of the mullet and linking the trend partly to lockdowns and closed salons.[2] The Rachel itself resurfaced in the early 2020s, helped by Friends: The Reunion in 2021, including a Modern Rachel version.[3]
